newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican workers play politics to demand wage hikes.
newsitem.headline: Mexican workers play politics to demand wage hikes.

text.p: With political pressures mounting against the government of President Ernesto Zedillo, once-docile Mexican workers are using carrot-and-stick tactics to seek an end in 1997 to years of falling real wages.

Using the veiled threat of the ballot box, top labour groups have begun to press for real wage increases in the approach to the renewal of Mexico's long-standing "Pacto", the year-end haggle between government, business and labour leaders to regulate wages and prices for the coming year.

Earlier this week, Enrique Aguilar Borrego, vice president of Mexico's largest union umbrella group, the Labour Congress, said workers would press for a 20 percent salary increase next year, reversing what he sees as 19 years of real declines.
If they failed to get it, he warned, Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 67 years, may pay the price in key mid-term congressional elections next year.

"What he was saying was that if the workers don't start recuperating purchasing power on the eve of the elections, obviously the opposition is going to take advantage," the Congress' spokesman, Enrique Escobar, told Reuters.
"The stomach doesn't understand macroeconomics. It understands that it has to eat."

Largely pro-government labour affiliations like the Labour Congress, representing some 45 percent of Mexico's 38-million-strong work force, have long delivered millions of votes for the PRI, giving Mexico a tradition of labour stability virtually unique across Latin America.
For many years, the payback was paltry wage hikes that mostly served to help Mexico achieve its goal of low-inflation economic stability.
But last year, when a December 1994 peso devaluation plunged the country into its worst recession in 50 years, patience, already wearing thin, began to snap.

Big unions like those of the telephone, teachers and electricity workers have threatened to desert pro-government labour confederations, suggesting consensus wage settlements may not be such a shoo-in as in the past.
Also, the emergence of a new group of armed guerrillas in the last 2-1/2 months in southern Mexico has put the government on notice that social unrest partially fuelled by poverty is on the rise.

Some economists are doubtful the government will cave in to the demands for steep wage hikes, trapped by the need to maintain its grip on inflation even though it badly needs to stoke private consumption to foster an economic recovery.
Others, however, say there is room for some flexibility.

"I would say one of the key anchors of the government's programme is the low wage costs. That is making Mexico attractive (to investors)," said Alfredo Thorne, economist at J.P. Morgan in Mexico City.
"But if the government returns a bit of the real wage erosion, that will be wonderful."
Business leaders have so far avoided the fray, saying they see no need to renegotiate the Pacto, known officially as the Alliance for Economic Recovery, until the end of the year.
The Labour Congress is expecting an agreement by mid-October. The approaching date has put investors on alert for any signs of inflationary pressure.
This week, Mexican social security workers won a 25 percent pay increase for next year -- far in excess of projected inflation in 1997 that many see around 13 percent.
But the size of that increase was offset by the fact the union failed to get a 12.5 percent "emergency" pay increase granted most other government workers in April.

Adding fuel to workers' demands, Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles recently told Congress he badly needed to raise electricity rates, a move that would set off a chain reaction of related price increases through the economy.
